title: Gray Minithyrotomy with Fat Implantation for Vocal Fold Scar and Sulcus
source_label: Operative Techniques in Laryngology (Rubin, Sataloff, Korovin 2024)
indications: Vocal fold scar or sulcus deformity with loss of superficial lamina propria pliability, stiff cover and poor mucosal wave, in a patient with normal vocal fold mobility who has failed voice therapy. A small window drilled through the thyroid cartilage gives access to the subepithelial plane without a mucosal incision, allowing release of the scar and implantation of autologous fat along the length of the fold under endoscopic view. It is not a treatment for paralysis or atrophy-related glottic insufficiency, and patients should expect improvement rather than a normal voice.
setup: Stroboscopy mapping the stiff segment; voice therapy completed.
Counsel that results vary and may fade if fat resorbs.
General anesthesia with 5.0 cuffed tube; IV dexamethasone 10-12 mg before starting.
Suspension laryngoscope with draped arm, 0- and 30-degree telescopes, continuous video visible to surgeon and assistant.
1-3 mm cutting burr, 22-27 g needles, Marchal dilator, Gimmick elevator, Bellucci scissors, alligator forceps, fibrin glue or bone wax.
Optional 16 g angiocatheter and 3 mL syringe for fat injection.
landmarks: Thyroid prow at the glottic level
Minithyrotomy 3-5 mm off midline at fold level
Long axis of the vocal fold toward the vocal process
danger: Drilling perpendicular to the lamina instead of along the fold axis
Large epithelial tear causing graft extrusion
Oversized pocket letting the graft migrate superolaterally
steps: Indication and expectations

Use for loss of cover pliability (scar or sulcus) with normal fold motion. It accesses the subepithelial plane without an epithelial incision but does not fix epithelium and gives little medialization, so it is not a paralysis or atrophy operation. Counsel that results can fade if fat resorbs.
Anesthesia

Use general anesthesia for stillness. Intubate with a 5.0 cuffed tube so the whole membranous fold is visible, and give 10-12 mg IV dexamethasone before starting, because edema builds quickly during full-length dissection.
Suspend and inspect

Suspend a laryngoscope that shows the anterior commissure to the vocal process. Inspect with a 0-degree (or 30-degree) telescope and correlate with stroboscopy. Make sure the scope tip does not evert the folds and distort where the vibratory edge appears.
Set up video and drape

Drape the suspension arm, which will be bumped. Run continuous video through the microscope or an assistant-held telescope, with monitors visible to both surgeon and assistant. A right-handed surgeon usually works from the patient's right.
Neck incision

Make a 2-3 cm horizontal incision over the thyroid prow at the expected glottic level. Divide the straps in the midline and sweep tissue off the cartilage with a Kittner, using cautery sparingly to protect the fat.
Harvest the fat
Take fat from the incision area, no more than 1-2 mL per fold, as homogeneous strips about the length of the fold (8-15 mm). Handle it gently, avoid heat, trim fascial strands, and keep it in saline.
Elevate perichondrium

Incise the outer perichondrium of the thyroid cartilage in the midline and elevate it superolaterally to expose about 1 cm2 on each side of the prow. Keep the flap intact so it can be laid back over the minithyrotomy at closure.
Needle-localize the glottis

Pass the finest needle that will penetrate (27 g, working up to 22 g) through the midline thyroid cartilage while the assistant watches it enter near the anterior commissure. Reposition until the glottic level is confirmed and mark it; with experience, angle the needle to rehearse the tunnel path.
Drill the minithyrotomy

Center a 1-3 mm cutting burr about 3-5 mm off midline at fold level, and angle the tunnel along the long axis of the fold, oblique rather than perpendicular to the lamina. Stop as soon as the inner cortex gives, and smooth the inner edge with a middle ear curette to avoid a saucerized hole.
Enter the subepithelial plane
Enter gently with a blunt fine probe such as a Marchal dilator, confirming endoscopically that its tip lies just under the epithelium. This orients you to the plane and the fold's axis.
Release the scar

Dissect mostly with blunt tympanoplasty instruments such as the Gimmick elevator; the sharp duckbill can easily tear mucosa. Reserve Bellucci scissors for dense adhesions. Pinhole perforations are acceptable, but stop and return later if there is a large tear.
Limit the pocket

Keep the pocket to the diseased segment mapped on stroboscopy and palpation. Normal superficial lamina propria separates very easily, and an oversized pocket, especially one running laterally onto the superior surface, lets the graft migrate under phonatory forces.
Place the fat

Insert one strip per side. Pull its leading (posterior) edge with alligator forceps and push with a probe, while the assistant smooths the medial edge with a microinstrument. Alternatively, inject the fat through a 16-gauge angiocatheter sheath from a 3 mL syringe. Do not undercorrect, since too little fat causes most failures.
Close and recover

Seal the tunnel with fibrin glue or bone wax, lay back the perichondrium, irrigate, and close, adding a rubber band drain only if needed. Discharge the same day on steroids with head elevation and a week of voice rest. Expect about a month of phonatory recovery, with review at 2-4 weeks.
exit_check: Pocket limited to the diseased segment with fat filling it
Epithelium intact or only pinhole perforations
postop: Phonatory recovery of about a month; monitor for late fade from fat resorption

late: Persistent stiffness from epithelial or deep changes

attending_followup: What layer is targeted by the Gray minithyrotomy?
The superficial lamina propria (Reinke space), the layer lost or scarred in sulcus and scar.
Why angle the minithyrotomy along the axis of the fold?
Dissection must run lengthwise along the fold; a perpendicular tunnel gives poor reach and risks perforation.
Why is this not an operation for vocal fold paralysis?
It provides little medialization; paralysis needs injection, thyroplasty or reinnervation.
What is the most common reason for failure?
Too little fat placed, so undercorrection should be avoided.
Name the sulcus types and which most impairs vibration.
Type I physiologic, type II sulcus vergeture and type III sulcus vocalis; types II and III are pathologic, with type III, extending into the ligament, the most severe.
